solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Not a complete arse — though decapitated farm animals

parts.note: but is the little word that does the work of though
the animals kept on a farm are stock, and the head letter is cut away

explanation.surface: A man judged not a complete idiot, beside some farm animals that have lost their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arse' does double duty: the insult the surface throws, and the anatomy the definition means one half of. Stock for the animals on a farm is the word hiding inside livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: An arse is two cheeks, so one of them falls short of a complete one — the definition names the part by what it is missing.

clue.text: In the sack, drunk starts to take exercise — potty!

indicators.note: In places the drunk and the starting letters inside the word for the sack

parts.note: the sack is slang for bed
a sot is a habitual drunk

indicators.note: starts to points to the first letters of take and exercise

parts.note: the first letters of take and exercise are T and E

explanation.surface: A drunk in bed is told to take some exercise, which seems crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' looks like an adjective but is the noun; 'starts to' takes only initials, and 'In the sack' wraps the bed round the rest. The exclamation 'potty!' is the definition, not a comment.
explanation.definitionFit: To be potty about someone is to be crazy about them, which is what besotted means: infatuated.

clue.text: Chuck's worth getting stuffed

indicators.note: Stuffing a thing crams its contents in at any angle, so the letters end up in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A man called Chuck deserves to be stuffed, like a trophy on a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' is placed to look like a name and is a verb. The indicator is the rude sense of stuffed, which does exactly the job any politer word for cramming would do.
explanation.definitionFit: To chuck something is to throw it — the everyday British verb for lobbing a thing away.

clue.text: Colleague needs right air to be suitable

parts.note: oppo is British slang for a workmate, short for opposite number
r is the standard short form for right
an air is a melody

explanation.surface: A colleague needs the right atmosphere before he will do.
explanation.walkthrough: An air is a tune in the old musical sense, the word behind 'Air on a G String'; the surface reads it as atmosphere instead. Oppo for a colleague is forces and police slang.
explanation.definitionFit: What is opportune suits the moment exactly, so a well-timed offer is a suitable one.

clue.text: As Keir represented Bill?

indicators.note: To re-present something is to present it afresh in another arrangement, which is what these letters get.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer standing in for a man called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilhelm II, Germany's emperor through the First World War, was Bill to the British press, and his title is what the clue is after. Keir is Sir Keir Starmer, Labour's prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain nicknamed Wilhelm II 'Bill', so the name on its own stands for the German emperor's title, kaiser.

clue.text: Friday commandeered by mad Crusoe to adjust telescope?

indicators.note: Something commandeered has been seized and carried off by whoever took it, so this letter joins the letters that follow.
A mad thing has lost its proper order, and letters out of their proper order have to be rearranged.

parts.note: f is the day's short form on a timetable
anagram fodder, six letters, with the day's letter joined in

explanation.surface: A deranged Robinson Crusoe seizes Man Friday and fiddles with his telescope.
explanation.walkthrough: Friday is Crusoe's companion in Defoe's novel and here supplies nothing but the weekday's initial. The question mark concedes that a telescope is only one of the things you might do this to.
explanation.definitionFit: To refocus is to reset a lens until the image comes back sharp, which is the adjustment a telescope keeps needing.

clue.text: Wifeless like Lee Anderson and making amends

indicators.note: Less on the end of a word means without, so the letter that stands for a wife is taken out of the description that follows.

parts.note: Lee Anderson is chairman of Reform UK and sits on the hard right of British politics
w is the standard short form for wife, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: Lee Anderson, with no wife, is busy putting things right.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of the wordplay is one hyphenated description of the man, a letter lighter. Anderson chairs Reform UK, Nigel Farage's party, and is a byword in Britain for the hard right.
explanation.definitionFit: Righting a wrong is setting it straight again, which is what making amends amounts to.

clue.text: Gross Washington religious order

parts.note: a gross figure is a fat one
WA is the US postal code for Washington state

explanation.surface: A disgusting religious decree comes out of Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: Washington here is the state rather than the capital or the president, and its two-letter postal code is all the clue takes. 'Gross' wants the plain adjective for fat, not the surface's revulsion.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatwa is a ruling handed down by an Islamic authority, so it is an order issued on religious grounds.

clue.text: Mistress sure to rot in jail

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the slang word for jail

parts.note: can is slang for prison, especially in the US

indicators.note: to rot is to decay and fall apart, so the letters of sure to fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A kept woman is certain to end up rotting in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rot' reads as the fate of the mistress, but it is the instruction to rearrange 'sure to', and 'in jail' sets the result inside an American slang word for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A courtesan is a woman kept by wealthy lovers, historically a high-class mistress.

clue.text: Gorgeous detective casually mounts bishop

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever mounts climbs on top, so the letters before it are written above the letter that follows.

parts.note: a police superintendent is the super in casual speech
b is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

explanation.surface: An off-duty detective climbing on top of a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casually' is not padding: it licenses the clipped form of superintendent that officers actually use. The mounting is vertical, which is the only direction a down entry offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb means of the finest quality, which is the claim calling a thing gorgeous makes.

clue.text: Strong and into S and M?

definitions.note: The second half describes a person's taste rather than defining a word: what someone into S and M is into is the noun, the use of straps, while the first half is the adjective for big and well-built.
definitions.meaning: the sense used of a big, well-built lad rather than of a taste or a drink
sadomasochism runs on whips, chains and straps, and the noun names the use of them

explanation.surface: A big strong type who is also keen on whips and chains.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are definitions, which is why nothing in the clue asks for a letter to be moved. S and M is sadomasochism, and the second half teases rather than defines — Cyclops's usual register.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapping lad is powerfully built, and strapping is also the business of straps that sadomasochism turns on.

clue.text: (& 11ac.) Old fart, one who pulls president's erection

parts.note: an old word for breaking wind
whoever tows a thing is the one doing the towing, the agent noun said with a long o

explanation.surface: An old fart turns out to be the one tugging at the president's erection.
explanation.walkthrough: The second piece is the agent noun from 'tow' — one who tows — said with a long o. The definition carries the joke: an erection is anything put up, and this president put his name on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump Tower is the Manhattan skyscraper Donald Trump built and named after himself, so the president's erection is literally his own building.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Fan, say, of T.Rex screwed by player

indicators.note: screwed means twisted, so the letters of the band name are rearranged

parts.note: the band name T.Rex supplies the four letters T, R, E and X
an actor is a player on stage

explanation.surface: A fan of the glam-rock band T.Rex is seduced by an actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan' looks like an admirer of T.Rex, the 1970s glam-rock band, but it is the kind of fan in a kitchen or bathroom; 'screwed' rearranges the band's name into EXTR.
explanation.definitionFit: An extractor fan draws stale air or steam out of a room, so a fan is one example of an extractor.

clue.text: Topless, weepy, getting a bollocking

indicators.note: Something topless has lost its top, and the top of a word is the letter it begins with.

parts.note: someone weepy is tearful, and the top letter then goes

explanation.surface: A topless woman in tears is being told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' plays both its senses at once: the Private Eye picture and the instruction to drop a first letter. A bollocking is British slang for a fierce dressing-down.
explanation.definitionFit: An earful is a torrent of abuse poured into somebody's ear, which is what a bollocking delivers.

clue.text: Balance requires EU supporter to accept date

indicators.note: To accept a thing is to take it in, so the letter named after it goes inside the word before.

parts.note: in the Brexit argument those who wanted Britain to stay in the EU were Remainers
d is the standard short form for date

explanation.surface: A pro-EU campaigner has to agree to a date.
explanation.walkthrough: Remainer was the label for the anti-Brexit side in the 2016 referendum, and it has to be read as one word rather than a phrase. 'Balance' wants the accountant's sense: what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The remainder is what is left once the rest has been taken away, which is the balance of a sum or an account.

clue.text: Powerful trendy present, maybe

parts.note: what is in is what is fashionable
the present is one of the tenses, which is what maybe concedes

explanation.surface: A gift that happens to be fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the grammarian's tense here rather than the parcel, and 'maybe' is in the clue because the present is only one tense among several.
explanation.definitionFit: An intense heat or an intense effort is a concentrated one, which is what calling it powerful says.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) Overexcited, rue going bananas for Trump-style legislation

indicators.note: To go bananas is to go completely wild, and letters gone wild have to be put back in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Regret goes berserk in the excitement over the president's way of making law.
explanation.walkthrough: An executive order is a presidential decree that bypasses Congress, so 'Trump-style legislation' is a jab as well as a definition. 'Rue' is the noun — regret — which is what keeps the surface upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump governs by executive order, signing decrees that do the work of law without Congress ever voting.

clue.text: Labour dupe agitated and upset

parts.note: labour means work

indicators.note: agitated means shaken up, so the letters of dupe are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Labour Party, duped and stirred up, is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party, but it is plain toil; 'agitated' turns dupe into EDUP.
explanation.definitionFit: Worked up describes someone agitated or distressed, an idiom for being upset.

clue.text: Bully, whiskey-covered Republican, put away

indicators.note: In a down clue what covers a thing lies over the top of it, so these letters are written above the letter that follows.

parts.note: a single malt is whiskey
R is the party's letter beside a candidate's name on a US ballot
to put food away is to eat it

explanation.surface: A Republican drenched in whiskey is bullied and then locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' is imprisonment in the surface and eating in the wordplay. The covering is vertical: in a down entry the whiskey lies over the party letter rather than wrapping round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To maltreat someone is to handle them cruelly, which is what a bully does to a victim.

clue.text: English politician at fault dropping Reform's first leader

indicators.note: Dropping a letter takes it out of what has been assembled so far.
The first of a name is the letter it starts with, and that is the letter named here.

parts.note: e is the standard short form for English
an MP is a Member of Parliament
someone at fault is in error, with one letter then taken out
the opening letter of Reform UK, Nigel Farage's party, and the letter dropped

explanation.surface: An English MP in the wrong after Reform's first leader is dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Reform UK is Nigel Farage's party and the clue takes only the R it starts with. 'Leader' is the definition, sitting at the end of a sentence about party leadership so that it reads as part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the man at the head of an empire, so he is a leader in the plainest sense of the word.

clue.text: Protrusion of organ: the woman's in a whirl

indicators.note: A whirl spins whatever is caught up in it, so these letters come to rest in a different order.

parts.note: what belongs to the woman is hers, and her is that possessive
the three letters of in a in another order

explanation.surface: A woman is in a spin about somebody's organ.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is two words a solver reads straight past — 'in a' — and the colon does nothing beyond staging the surface. 'The woman's' wants the possessive pronoun, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A hernia is an organ pushing out through the wall that should contain it, which is exactly a protrusion of organ.

clue.text: Bling, perhaps, offered by streetwise guy round church

parts.note: bro is street slang for a mate
the letter drawn as a circle
ch is how church is abbreviated on a map

explanation.surface: A street-smart lad hands over some jewellery outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like the preposition that would wrap one piece about another and is simply the letter shaped like a circle. Bling is 1990s hip-hop slang for showy jewellery, which 'perhaps' narrows to one item.
explanation.definitionFit: A brooch is a jewelled pin worn to be noticed, so it counts as bling — 'perhaps' conceding it is only one kind.

clue.text: Rock's at London university, failing that

parts.note: ore is the rock a metal is dug out of
the London School of Economics, on Houghton Street off the Strand

explanation.surface: Rock music has made it onto the syllabus at a London university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' is the geologist's here, not the guitarist's. LSE is the London School of Economics, whose initials are the standard shorthand for a London university.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Or else' is how an ultimatum ends — do this, failing that, and here is what follows.

clue.text: One claiming to cause downfall of Iran — fantastic supreme being!

indicators.note: Something fantastic is wildly out of the ordinary, and letters out of their ordinary order have to be rearranged.

parts.note: the four letters of Iran in another order
the Maker is God, as in 'meet your Maker'

explanation.surface: A man boasts that he can bring Iran down, and salutes a fantastic god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' is a regime's collapse in the surface and the falling of rain in the definition. The exclamation mark belongs to the surface's enthusiasm and carries no instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainmaker claims to bring the rain down, by ritual or by seeding clouds, so the downfall promised is the weather's.

clue.text: Often seen before Christmas, pissed

definitions.note: The first half does not define the word at all but says where it is usually printed — immediately in front of Christmas — which is fair play as long as the other half is a true synonym.
definitions.meaning: the word that heads the greeting on every card in the shop
British slang for drunk, and the other half of the clue wants the politer word for that state

explanation.surface: Drunk in the weeks running up to Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: One half is a synonym and the other is a position: the word wanted is the one that habitually stands in front of 'Christmas'. 'Pissed' is British for drunk, not the American sense of annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Merry is the word that always precedes Christmas in the greeting, and merry is also long-standing British slang for tipsy.

clue.text: Finished sexual initiation with alien — pissed off

parts.note: when time is up it is finished

indicators.note: An initiation is a beginning, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of sexual
ET is the film's extra-terrestrial and the crossword's standard alien

explanation.surface: A first sexual experience with an extraterrestrial, now over, has left somebody annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiation' reads as a first sexual experience and asks for a first letter. 'Finished' wants the up of 'time's up', which is how two letters come out of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone upset has been put out and is smarting about it, which is what pissed off says more bluntly.

clue.text: Poles, in picture, smell?

indicators.note: 'in' names the place a thing goes, so the letters before it are set inside the word that follows.

parts.note: to picture a thing is to see it in the mind
N and S are the two poles of a magnet or a compass

explanation.surface: Some Poles turn up in a photograph and apparently smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P offers Polish people and the clue means the magnetic pair. 'Smell?' is a definition by example — one of the five — with the question mark admitting as much.
explanation.definitionFit: Smell is one of the five senses, so the clue names the class by a single member of it.

clue.text: see 16dn.
Trifling Democrat coalition

parts.note: D is the party's letter beside a candidate's name on a US ballot
an alliance is a coalition of parties or powers

explanation.surface: A Democrat's unimportant coalition deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifling' is the noun — the act of trifling — and not the adjective meaning trivial that the surface offers. A dalliance can be a flirtation or merely a half-hearted go at something.
explanation.definitionFit: A dalliance is dabbling or flirting, so trifling, the act of not taking a thing seriously, names it.

clue.text: Press on about Murphy losing head without Rugby Union backing

indicators.note: without means outside, so the rearranged letters go round the reversed abbreviation
about suggests turning things round in any direction, so the remaining letters are rearranged
losing head means the first letter of Murphy is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, the surname Murphy

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the abbreviation is read in reverse

explanation.surface: Someone presses on about a headless Murphy, with no backing from Rugby Union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' but rearranges what is left of Murphy after 'losing head'; 'backing' turns the Rugby Union abbreviation round, and 'without', in its old sense of outside, wraps the jumble round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurry up and press on both mean carry on more quickly, an idiomatic match.

clue.text: Keele men try storing carbon?

indicators.note: Something storing another thing keeps it whole inside itself, so the letters sit unbroken in the words before.

parts.note: the seven letters run on without a break across the three words

explanation.surface: Men at Keele University are trying to store carbon.
explanation.walkthrough: Keele is a university in Staffordshire, and the run begins inside its name — three ordinary words with a seam in the middle of the first. 'Carbon?' names one member of the class, which the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon is one of the chemical elements, so the clue points at the class by naming a single example of it.
